title: Golang Maps: How Swiss Tables Replaced the Old Bucket Design
excerpt: Go 1.24 replaces the old bucket-and-overflow map internals with a Swiss Table-inspired design to improve cache locality, lookup speed, and memory efficiency.
content_html:
Introduction

Maps sit on the hot path of almost every non-trivial Go program: they power request routing, cache lookups, deduplication sets, aggregation pipelines, and a lot of the glue code we barely notice until it gets slow. Because they are so common, even small runtime-level improvements in map behavior can produce measurable gains across real systems.

Go 1.24 shipped one of the biggest map-internals changes in years: the classic bucket-plus-overflow implementation has been replaced by a Swiss Table-inspired design. The external API did not change, your code still writes map[K]V and calls make, indexing, delete, and range the same way as before. Under the hood, however, lookup and insert paths were reshaped around tighter metadata, flatter probing patterns, and much better cache locality.

The practical effect is straightforward: less pointer chasing, fewer cache misses, higher useful load factors, and faster common operations in many workloads. In microbenchmarks this can be dramatic, while full applications usually see smaller but still meaningful aggregate wins. Memory behavior also improves in many scenarios, especially where old overflow chains used to accumulate.

This post focuses on what changed specifically in Go's runtime design, why those choices matter, and where the trade-offs still show up. If you want a conceptual refresher on hash tables first, see Hash Map Deep Dive.

Go's Old Map Implementation (Pre-1.24)

Before Go 1.24, maps used a bucketed design that had been refined for years and worked well for a wide range of workloads. Each map owned an array of buckets. Each bucket held up to 8 key/value pairs, plus metadata used to speed up matching and track slot state. When a bucket filled up, the runtime allocated an overflow bucket and chained it to the original one.

At a high level, the layout looked like this:

The key idea was simple and practical. Hash the key, use part of the hash to pick the bucket, then scan that bucket's entries. If no matching key was found and an overflow bucket existed, keep walking the chain until the key was found or the chain ended.

In simplified form, the core structures were roughly:

// Conceptual shape, not the exact runtime source.
type hmap struct {   // map header
	count      int
	B          uint8   // number of buckets is 1<<B
	buckets    *bmap
	oldbuckets *bmap   // previous bucket array during growth
}

type bmap struct {   // bucket with 8 slots
	tophash  [8]uint8
	keys     [8]K
	values   [8]V
	overflow *bmap
}

This design had real strengths: it was stable, battle-tested, and supported incremental growth so resize work did not arrive as one huge latency spike. During growth, the map kept both old and new bucket arrays for a while, and operations gradually evacuated old buckets into their new positions as the map was accessed.

The main cost was memory locality under pressure. Overflow chains introduced pointer chasing, and pointer chasing means cache misses. Once hot buckets started spilling into overflow, lookups and inserts could bounce across non-contiguous memory. The implementation also had practical load-factor limits around 81 percent (roughly 6.5 filled slots per 8-slot bucket) before growth pressure and collision costs became harder to ignore.

So the old map was not a broken design waiting to be replaced, but an effective implementation with trade-offs that became more visible as modern CPUs, cache behavior, and high-throughput services pushed for tighter, flatter probe paths.

Swiss Tables: Core Design

Historically, Swiss Tables came out of Google's internal performance work on hash tables and were later documented and open-sourced through Abseil — Google's open-source C++ library collection — as flat_hash_map and related containers. The design notes are still the best primary reference for the model and its trade-offs.

Swiss Tables keep the same high-level hash-table contract, but reorganize the data path around two ideas: compact per-slot metadata and probe-friendly contiguous groups. The design has since been adopted across several runtimes and databases because it moves the common-case probe work onto a much more cache-efficient path.

The first thing to understand is that Swiss Tables do not start probing by reading full keys. They start by reading metadata bytes that are cheap to scan in bulk. Only candidates survive to full key comparison. This sounds small, but it changes where CPU time goes.

Hash split: one part for placement, one part for filtering

A key is hashed once, then split into two logical pieces:

  • h1: used to choose the initial group index.
  • h2: a short fingerprint stored in per-slot metadata.

You can think of h2 as a fast pre-check. If a slot's fingerprint does not match, there is no reason to touch that slot's key bytes at all. Most probes end up rejecting many slots at this metadata stage, which is much cheaper than repeatedly loading and comparing full keys.

Group-oriented layout

Instead of treating each slot as an isolated unit, Swiss Tables organize slots into fixed-size groups. In Go's design, that group size is 8 slots, which aligns with compact metadata handling and practical cache behavior.

Each group stores:

  • a control word (one metadata byte per slot, packed together),
  • 8 key slots,
  • 8 value slots.

Conceptually:

group i:
	ctrl: [c0 c1 c2 c3 c4 c5 c6 c7]
	keys: [k0 k1 k2 k3 k4 k5 k6 k7]
	vals: [v0 v1 v2 v3 v4 v5 v6 v7]

Control bytes encode slot state (empty, deleted, occupied) and, for occupied slots, include the h2 fingerprint bits. Because those 8 control bytes are contiguous, the runtime can inspect all slot states for a group in one tight operation.

Probe sequence: filter first, compare keys second

Lookup becomes a two-stage loop:

  1. Read the current group's control bytes.
  2. Find control-byte positions whose fingerprints match h2.
  3. For those positions only, compare real keys.
  4. If no match, advance to the next group in the probe sequence.
  5. Stop when an empty slot proves the key is absent.

Simplified pseudocode:

g = startGroup(h1)
for {
	matches = matchFingerprint(ctrl[g], h2)
	for each pos in matches {
		if keys[g][pos] == key {
			return vals[g][pos]
		}
	}

	if hasEmpty(ctrl[g]) {
		return not found
	}

	g = nextGroup(g)
}

The hasEmpty(ctrl[g]) check is key. In open addressing, an empty slot means probing can terminate: if the key had ever been inserted along this sequence, the probe would have encountered it before the first truly empty slot.

Insertion and the role of deleted slots

Insert follows the same probe path used by lookup, but it tracks the first reusable position it sees. Reusable can mean either:

  • an empty slot, or
  • a deleted slot (tombstone), depending on policy and probe progress.

When lookup fails to find the key, insert writes into the best reusable slot discovered so far. This preserves probe invariants while limiting uncontrolled cluster growth.

Deletion does not usually compact the cluster immediately. Instead, it marks metadata as deleted. Immediate compaction would make single deletes expensive and can break probe continuity guarantees. The trade-off is that too many tombstones can lengthen future probes, so implementations need cleanup behavior during growth or reorganization phases.

Why this maps well to modern CPUs

Swiss Tables are often described as "SIMD-friendly," but the broader point is locality plus branch behavior:

  • Contiguous metadata scan: a group's control bytes are read together, reducing scattered memory touches.
  • Fewer full key loads: most slots fail at fingerprint stage, so key comparisons are sparse.
  • Predictable hot loop: probe steps are simple and repetitive, helping branch prediction.
  • Better cache residency: metadata and nearby slots are packed to favor cache lines.

Even without architecture-specific vector instructions, this shape tends to perform better than pointer-heavy traversals once maps reach realistic production sizes.

Load factor and practical ceiling

The old bucket-overflow model had to balance overflow growth costs relatively early. Swiss-style open addressing tolerates denser occupancy before performance degrades sharply, because probe work remains mostly linear scans over compact metadata and nearby slots.

In practice, this pushes useful load factors upward into the high-80% range (often discussed around 87.5% for 8-slot group designs). The exact threshold is implementation-dependent, but the key result is consistent: denser tables are possible before lookups and inserts become too expensive.

Higher usable density means less memory overhead per stored entry and fewer growth events for the same number of elements — both effects that show up directly in heap profiles and allocation rates.

The trade-offs do not disappear

Swiss Tables are not universally faster in every corner case. At high tombstone density or under specific delete-heavy patterns, probe lengths can regress until cleanup or growth restores table quality. Extremely adversarial hash distributions still hurt any open-addressing design, even with strong metadata filtering.

The improvement comes from moving the common case onto a much more cache-efficient path, not from eliminating all hard cases.

That is why the shift matters so much for Go: maps are used everywhere, and the common case is where most CPU cycles are spent.

Go-Specific Adaptations

If this were only a straightforward port of Abseil-style Swiss Tables, the runtime work would have been simpler. Go maps, however, have constraints that come from language behavior, GC integration, and long-standing expectations around latency and iteration. The interesting part of Go 1.24 is not just adopting Swiss-style probing, but adapting it so those constraints still hold.

Growth without long stop-the-world style spikes

Classic open-addressing tables are often resized by allocating a larger table and reinserting everything in one large migration step. That is fine in some systems, but Go maps are used on hot request paths where single-operation latency matters. A resize strategy that occasionally performs a full-table rehash can create exactly the kind of long tail the runtime tries to avoid.

Go's adaptation avoids that monolithic jump by spreading growth across smaller units. Instead of treating the map as one giant table that doubles and fully rehashes at once, the runtime can split work so expansion happens incrementally. Operationally, this keeps mutation costs more stable because a single insert is less likely to inherit the full cost of moving every existing element.

The practical effect is similar in spirit to the old map's gradual evacuation model: growth still happens, but migration work is amortized across normal operations rather than concentrated into one expensive event.

Multiple independent tables and directory-style routing

One of the key Go-specific choices is to organize storage as multiple smaller Swiss-style tables rather than one ever-growing monolith. A higher-level directory (conceptually similar to extendible hashing) routes keys to a specific table segment, and only the segment under pressure needs to split.

Keeping growth local means hot key regions can expand without forcing a global rebuild, and bounding memory movement to the splitting segment improves latency predictability under write-heavy bursts.

At a conceptual level, insertion looks like this:

hash key
use high bits to select table segment
probe within that segment's Swiss groups
if segment exceeds thresholds, split that segment and update directory

That directory update is much cheaper than rebuilding every segment, and it composes well with Go's preference for incremental runtime work.

Preserving Go's range semantics while tables change

One of the hardest constraints is preserving Go's map iteration behavior while inserts, deletes, and growth are happening.

In Go, iterating with range over a map has deliberately loose ordering guarantees, but it still has safety and consistency expectations. The runtime cannot expose torn state, lose reachability to entries that should still be visible under the language rules, or let relocation mechanics violate iterator correctness.

With segmented Swiss-style storage, this means iterators must understand that entries may move as segments split or internal probe layouts change. The runtime therefore couples iteration state to map-internal versioning and traversal metadata so the iterator can continue safely even while structure evolves.

The implementation details are complex, but the user-visible result is simple: for k, v := range m keeps working while the runtime earns better cache locality and denser storage under the hood.

GC and write-barrier friendliness

Go cannot treat table entries as purely mechanical bytes. Keys and values may contain pointers, and pointer movement interacts with garbage collection and write barriers. Any redesign of map internals must preserve accurate pointer visibility and barrier behavior during insert, delete, grow, and iterator transitions.

Segmented growth helps here too. Smaller relocation steps are easier to integrate with barriered writes and reduce the size of any single pointer-moving operation. This does not remove complexity, but it narrows blast radius and keeps runtime bookkeeping more tractable.

Swiss-style metadata probing delivers the raw algorithmic win, but Go-specific adaptations — segmented growth, iterator-safe migration, and GC-barrier integration — are what make that win usable at scale in a garbage-collected, latency-sensitive runtime. The performance numbers in the next section reflect both layers working together.

Performance & Memory Analysis (Deeper Dive)

The easiest way to get misled by map benchmarks is to look only at a single synthetic test and assume that number transfers directly to production. For Swiss maps in Go, the public data tells a more nuanced story: the micro-level wins are real and often large, the application-level aggregate win is smaller but still positive, and a few workload shapes do regress enough to deserve attention.

The official release notes for Go 1.24 report that runtime work, including the new Swiss map implementation, lowered CPU overhead by about 2 to 3 percent on average across a representative benchmark suite (Go 1.24 release notes, Runtime section). That is a whole-runtime number, not a map-only number, but it is useful as a reality check because it is measured across mixed workloads.

For map-focused results, the most concrete summary from the runtime team is in Michael Pratt's closing comment on the Swiss map tracking issue: large-map access and assignment were reported around 30 to 35 percent faster, iteration about 10 percent faster overall and up to about 60 percent faster on low-load large maps, while full-application benchmarks in Sweet showed a geometric-mean speedup around 1.5 percent (golang/go#54766 comment, Sweet benchmark suite).

That gap between "30 percent here" and "1.5 percent there" is exactly what we should expect. Microbenchmarks isolate map operations, keep code paths hot, and often stress one operation type at a time. Real services spend time in parsing, syscalls, RPC boundaries, scheduling, GC assists, and dozens of non-map code paths, so map wins are diluted unless maps dominate the profile.

There is also evidence that benchmark design itself can exaggerate or mask effects. In a follow-up issue about map benchmarking quality, the Go team called out branch-predictor-friendly key patterns, power-of-two map sizes, and benchmark harness overhead as distortions, then showed that changing benchmark structure altered observed deltas substantially (golang/go#70700). One concrete data point from those follow-ups is that a small-map lookup fix for unpredictable keys improved hit latency by roughly 1.7x (about 25ns to about 14ns in the posted numbers), with misses also improving by about 1.3x in the same benchmark set (CL 634396 summary in #70700).

On memory, two facts are well supported by public sources. First, Swiss-style probing can run at higher practical occupancy than the old overflow-chain design, which tends to reduce per-entry overhead in many cases (Abseil Swiss table design, golang/go#54766). Second, Go's early public Swiss-map benchmark summary reported memory reductions in a broad but workload-dependent range, described there as 0 to 25 percent in most cases, with specific notes about avoiding extra allocations when reusing fixed-size maps (performance summary in #54766).

The cautionary side however, is equally important. The Go team and users tracked several regressions or edge cases after the 1.24 rollout, especially around cold-cache behavior and sparse-large-map patterns. The open cold-cache tracking issue explains why directory indirection and multiple allocations can increase miss costs and discusses layout experiments aimed at that problem (golang/go#70835). A concrete external report in that thread from Prometheus benchmarking showed higher runtime.mapaccess1_fast64 CPU time on Go 1.24.2 versus 1.23 for that workload shape, which is exactly the kind of profile-specific behavior that can hide behind positive geomeans (Prometheus report in #70835).

clear(m) on large-capacity sparse maps is another example of non-uniform behavior. The issue discussion shows that clear cost can track allocated table size in some patterns, and runtime contributors discuss mitigations plus related CLs that skip unnecessary work on empty groups (golang/go#70617). In other words, Swiss maps improved many paths, but they did not erase every pathological corner on day one.

The practical interpretation is straightforward: if your service is lookup- or insert-heavy with medium to large maps, Go 1.24+ likely gives you a free speedup and often better memory efficiency. If your profile is dominated by cold misses, very sparse huge maps, or tight clear/reuse loops, you should measure directly on your workload and watch ongoing runtime work, because those are active optimization areas rather than solved history.

Practical Takeaways for Go Developers

Understanding where the new implementation earns its wins helps you make better profiling decisions, write map-friendly patterns, and calibrate what upgrading to 1.24+ will actually deliver for your specific service.

Where you will see the most impact

The gains are largest when maps are the actual bottleneck. Large maps with frequent access are the clearest case: lookup and insert speed up most noticeably once a map has enough entries to expose pointer-chasing and cache-miss costs in the old implementation. A service that maintains large in-memory lookup tables, a cache keyed on structured identifiers, or a concurrent-access pattern over many sharded maps all stand to benefit measurably.

Iteration over large but sparsely populated maps also improves significantly. The old design had to walk all buckets regardless of occupancy; Swiss-style control-byte metadata lets the runtime skip empty groups quickly. If your code uses range to scan or drain big maps, that path gets faster.

Memory-constrained services are another case worth measuring. Higher load factors and the elimination of overflow bucket chains can reduce heap pressure from map storage, which in turn reduces GC frequency and can improve heap efficiency across the board.

The gains are smallest for maps that are tiny (a handful of keys), dominated by cold access, or never escape the runtime's fast-path specialization for small integer and string keys. For those maps, the new design may be neutral or show small regressions in some microbenchmarks. In practice, if those maps are not showing up as hotspots in your profiles, the difference is rarely relevant.

Profiling map behavior in your service

If maps do appear in CPU profiles, runtime.mapaccess1, runtime.mapassign, runtime.mapiterinit, and related symbols are the functions to watch. A large fraction of CPU time in those symbols combined with a flat or slowly improving heap is a good signal that you are in the "before Swiss tables" performance regime, or that some of the known cold-cache edge cases are affecting you.

For memory, heap profiles can show whether map entries contribute disproportionately to live allocation. Go 1.24+ should help here in many workloads, but if you see large map allocations persisting after keys are deleted, it is worth remembering that Go maps still do not shrink their allocated backing storage after deletions. That has not changed.

A quick way to probe whether maps contribute meaningfully to a benchmark or production workload is to compare go tool pprof profiles between Go 1.23 and 1.24+ builds. The runtime-level speedup is automatic, but quantifying it for your own code tells you whether it is worth emphasizing or ignoring.

Delete patterns and the clear idiom

The one code-level pattern worth some thought involves heavy delete usage. If your hot path is a tight loop that repeatedly deletes and reinserts many keys, you are exercising the tombstone path inside each probe group. Swiss-style open addressing handles this correctly, but at high tombstone density probes lengthen until cleanup happens during growth or at table reorganization points. This is the same trade-off that exists in other open-addressing designs, and Go's implementation manages it without application involvement, but it does mean delete-dominated workloads may see less benefit than pure lookup or insert workloads.

The clear(m) idiom used to wipe and reuse a map is something else to be aware of. Go maps do not shrink their backing storage when cleared, so calling clear on a map that previously grew large does not release that memory. The cost of clear itself is proportional to the number of allocated groups in the current design, which can be expensive for maps that were once large but now hold few entries.

// This pattern is fine and common.
// clear(m) resets map entries without releasing backing storage.
// If the map previously held many keys, the next iteration of inserts
// skips re-allocation, which is the intent.
m := make(map[string]int)
for {
    populate(m)
    process(m)
    clear(m)   // fast if m is consistently sized; more expensive if m grew large once
}

If you use this pattern with maps that burst to large sizes and then shrink back, consider whether the cleared map's long-term backing size is actually appropriate, or whether creating a fresh map in those cases is preferable.

What the runtime might still change

There is ongoing work around map cold-cache behavior. Runtime contributors are actively experimenting with memory layout changes, including separating keys from values within groups (the GOEXPERIMENT=mapsplitgroup experiment tracked in #70835), and the cold-cache issue itself remains open for Go 1.27. These are not user-facing API changes, but they mean the performance profile of maps will continue to evolve.

SIMD-based control-byte scanning, which Abseil's C++ implementation uses on x86, is not currently part of Go's Swiss map path. As noted in the CockroachDB swiss README, implementing the probe loop in pure Go assembly with SIMD has non-trivial overhead from function call boundaries, and the Go team has taken a SWAR (SIMD Within A Register) approach instead. That may change in future versions as Go's assembly model and CPU support evolve.

Conclusion

Go 1.24's map redesign is a clear demonstration that significant improvements are still available in well-trodden code. The bucket-and-overflow model served Go programs reliably for years, and it was not replaced out of novelty but out of accumulated evidence that a Swiss Table-inspired layout could make the common case genuinely faster, with better memory efficiency, at production scale.

The core design choices, tighter group-level metadata, faster candidate filtering before full key comparisons, and a flat probe path, come directly from Abseil's Swiss Tables. What Go added on top is the runtime infrastructure that makes those choices safe and compatible with garbage collection, iterator semantics, and latency-sensitive growth. That second layer is less visible but equally important.

For developers, the change is mostly transparent. Upgrading to 1.24 or later is enough to pick up the improvements. The caveat is that aggregate production gains tend to be modest unless maps dominate your CPU profile, cold-access patterns can regress in specific shapes, and the runtime team is still iterating. Measure your actual workload rather than extrapolating from microbenchmark headlines.

Go continues to treat its runtime as something that can be improved through careful, verified engineering. The Swiss map work is a good example of that discipline: a multi-year effort across proposal, design, implementation, and benchmarking that ultimately shipped without changing the language surface at all.

Preserving Go's range semantics while tables change One of the hardest constraints is preserving Go's map iteration behavior while inserts, deletes, and growth are happening. In Go, iterating with range over a map has deliberately loose ordering guarantees, but it still has safety and consistency expectations. The runtime cannot expose torn state, lose reachability to entries that should still be visible under the language rules, or let relocation mechanics violate iterator correctness. With segmented Swiss-style storage, this means iterators must understand that entries may move as segments split or internal probe layouts change. The runtime therefore couples iteration state to map-internal versioning and traversal metadata so the iterator can continue safely even while structure evolves. The implementation details are complex, but the user-visible result is simple: for k, v := range m keeps working while the runtime earns better cache locality and denser storage under the hood. GC and write-barrier friendliness Go cannot treat table entries as purely mechanical bytes. Keys and values may contain pointers, and pointer movement interacts with garbage collection and write barriers. Any redesign of map internals must preserve accurate pointer visibility and barrier behavior during insert, delete, grow, and iterator transitions. Segmented growth helps here too. Smaller relocation steps are easier to integrate with barriered writes and reduce the size of any single pointer-moving operation. This does not remove complexity, but it narrows blast radius and keeps runtime bookkeeping more tractable. Swiss-style metadata probing delivers the raw algorithmic win, but Go-specific adaptations — segmented growth, iterator-safe migration, and GC-barrier integration — are what make that win usable at scale in a garbage-collected, latency-sensitive runtime. The performance numbers in the next section reflect both layers working together. Performance & Memory Analysis (Deeper Dive) The easiest way to get misled by map benchmarks is to look only at a single synthetic test and assume that number transfers directly to production. For Swiss maps in Go, the public data tells a more nuanced story: the micro-level wins are real and often large, the application-level aggregate win is smaller but still positive, and a few workload shapes do regress enough to deserve attention. The official release notes for Go 1.24 report that runtime work, including the new Swiss map implementation, lowered CPU overhead by about 2 to 3 percent on average across a representative benchmark suite (Go 1.24 release notes, Runtime section). That is a whole-runtime number, not a map-only number, but it is useful as a reality check because it is measured across mixed workloads. For map-focused results, the most concrete summary from the runtime team is in Michael Pratt's closing comment on the Swiss map tracking issue: large-map access and assignment were reported around 30 to 35 percent faster, iteration about 10 percent faster overall and up to about 60 percent faster on low-load large maps, while full-application benchmarks in Sweet showed a geometric-mean speedup around 1.5 percent (golang/go#54766 comment, Sweet benchmark suite). That gap between "30 percent here" and "1.5 percent there" is exactly what we should expect. Microbenchmarks isolate map operations, keep code paths hot, and often stress one operation type at a time. Real services spend time in parsing, syscalls, RPC boundaries, scheduling, GC assists, and dozens of non-map code paths, so map wins are diluted unless maps dominate the profile. There is also evidence that benchmark design itself can exaggerate or mask effects. In a follow-up issue about map benchmarking quality, the Go team called out branch-predictor-friendly key patterns, power-of-two map sizes, and benchmark harness overhead as distortions, then showed that changing benchmark structure altered observed deltas substantially (golang/go#70700). One concrete data point from those follow-ups is that a small-map lookup fix for unpredictable keys improved hit latency by roughly 1.7x (about 25ns to about 14ns in the posted numbers), with misses also improving by about 1.3x in the same benchmark set (CL 634396 summary in #70700). On memory, two facts are well supported by public sources. First, Swiss-style probing can run at higher practical occupancy than the old overflow-chain design, which tends to reduce per-entry overhead in many cases (Abseil Swiss table design, golang/go#54766). Second, Go's early public Swiss-map benchmark summary reported memory reductions in a broad but workload-dependent range, described there as 0 to 25 percent in most cases, with specific notes about avoiding extra allocations when reusing fixed-size maps (performance summary in #54766). The cautionary side however, is equally important. The Go team and users tracked several regressions or edge cases after the 1.24 rollout, especially around cold-cache behavior and sparse-large-map patterns. The open cold-cache tracking issue explains why directory indirection and multiple allocations can increase miss costs and discusses layout experiments aimed at that problem (golang/go#70835). A concrete external report in that thread from Prometheus benchmarking showed higher runtime.mapaccess1_fast64 CPU time on Go 1.24.2 versus 1.23 for that workload shape, which is exactly the kind of profile-specific behavior that can hide behind positive geomeans (Prometheus report in #70835). clear(m) on large-capacity sparse maps is another example of non-uniform behavior. The issue discussion shows that clear cost can track allocated table size in some patterns, and runtime contributors discuss mitigations plus related CLs that skip unnecessary work on empty groups (golang/go#70617). In other words, Swiss maps improved many paths, but they did not erase every pathological corner on day one. The practical interpretation is straightforward: if your service is lookup- or insert-heavy with medium to large maps, Go 1.24+ likely gives you a free speedup and often better memory efficiency. If your profile is dominated by cold misses, very sparse huge maps, or tight clear/reuse loops, you should measure directly on your workload and watch ongoing runtime work, because those are active optimization areas rather than solved history. Practical Takeaways for Go Developers Understanding where the new implementation earns its wins helps you make better profiling decisions, write map-friendly patterns, and calibrate what upgrading to 1.24+ will actually deliver for your specific service. Where you will see the most impact The gains are largest when maps are the actual bottleneck. Large maps with frequent access are the clearest case: lookup and insert speed up most noticeably once a map has enough entries to expose pointer-chasing and cache-miss costs in the old implementation. A service that maintains large in-memory lookup tables, a cache keyed on structured identifiers, or a concurrent-access pattern over many sharded maps all stand to benefit measurably. Iteration over large but sparsely populated maps also improves significantly. The old design had to walk all buckets regardless of occupancy; Swiss-style control-byte metadata lets the runtime skip empty groups quickly. If your code uses range to scan or drain big maps, that path gets faster. Memory-constrained services are another case worth measuring. Higher load factors and the elimination of overflow bucket chains can reduce heap pressure from map storage, which in turn reduces GC frequency and can improve heap efficiency across the board. The gains are smallest for maps that are tiny (a handful of keys), dominated by cold access, or never escape the runtime's fast-path specialization for small integer and string keys. For those maps, the new design may be neutral or show small regressions in some microbenchmarks. In practice, if those maps are not showing up as hotspots in your profiles, the difference is rarely relevant. Profiling map behavior in your service If maps do appear in CPU profiles, runtime.mapaccess1, runtime.mapassign, runtime.mapiterinit, and related symbols are the functions to watch. A large fraction of CPU time in those symbols combined with a flat or slowly improving heap is a good signal that you are in the "before Swiss tables" performance regime, or that some of the known cold-cache edge cases are affecting you. For memory, heap profiles can show whether map entries contribute disproportionately to live allocation. Go 1.24+ should help here in many workloads, but if you see large map allocations persisting after keys are deleted, it is worth remembering that Go maps still do not shrink their allocated backing storage after deletions. That has not changed. A quick way to probe whether maps contribute meaningfully to a benchmark or production workload is to compare go tool pprof profiles between Go 1.23 and 1.24+ builds. The runtime-level speedup is automatic, but quantifying it for your own code tells you whether it is worth emphasizing or ignoring. Delete patterns and the clear idiom The one code-level pattern worth some thought involves heavy delete usage. If your hot path is a tight loop that repeatedly deletes and reinserts many keys, you are exercising the tombstone path inside each probe group. Swiss-style open addressing handles this correctly, but at high tombstone density probes lengthen until cleanup happens during growth or at table reorganization points. This is the same trade-off that exists in other open-addressing designs, and Go's implementation manages it without application involvement, but it does mean delete-dominated workloads may see less benefit than pure lookup or insert workloads. The clear(m) idiom used to wipe and reuse a map is something else to be aware of. Go maps do not shrink their backing storage when cleared, so calling clear on a map that previously grew large does not release that memory. The cost of clear itself is proportional to the number of allocated groups in the current design, which can be expensive for maps that were once large but now hold few entries. // This pattern is fine and common. // clear(m) resets map entries without releasing backing storage. // If the map previously held many keys, the next iteration of inserts // skips re-allocation, which is the intent. m := make(map[string]int) for { populate(m) process(m) clear(m) // fast if m is consistently sized; more expensive if m grew large once } If you use this pattern with maps that burst to large sizes and then shrink back, consider whether the cleared map's long-term backing size is actually appropriate, or whether creating a fresh map in those cases is preferable. What the runtime might still change There is ongoing work around map cold-cache behavior. Runtime contributors are actively experimenting with memory layout changes, including separating keys from values within groups (the GOEXPERIMENT=mapsplitgroup experiment tracked in #70835), and the cold-cache issue itself remains open for Go 1.27. These are not user-facing API changes, but they mean the performance profile of maps will continue to evolve. SIMD-based control-byte scanning, which Abseil's C++ implementation uses on x86, is not currently part of Go's Swiss map path. As noted in the CockroachDB swiss README, implementing the probe loop in pure Go assembly with SIMD has non-trivial overhead from function call boundaries, and the Go team has taken a SWAR (SIMD Within A Register) approach instead. That may change in future versions as Go's assembly model and CPU support evolve. Conclusion Go 1.24's map redesign is a clear demonstration that significant improvements are still available in well-trodden code. The bucket-and-overflow model served Go programs reliably for years, and it was not replaced out of novelty but out of accumulated evidence that a Swiss Table-inspired layout could make the common case genuinely faster, with better memory efficiency, at production scale. The core design choices, tighter group-level metadata, faster candidate filtering before full key comparisons, and a flat probe path, come directly from Abseil's Swiss Tables. What Go added on top is the runtime infrastructure that makes those choices safe and compatible with garbage collection, iterator semantics, and latency-sensitive growth. That second layer is less visible but equally important. For developers, the change is mostly transparent. Upgrading to 1.24 or later is enough to pick up the improvements. The caveat is that aggregate production gains tend to be modest unless maps dominate your CPU profile, cold-access patterns can regress in specific shapes, and the runtime team is still iterating. Measure your actual workload rather than extrapolating from microbenchmark headlines. Go continues to treat its runtime as something that can be improved through careful, verified engineering. The Swiss map work is a good example of that discipline: a multi-year effort across proposal, design, implementation, and benchmarking that ultimately shipped without changing the language surface at all.

sentences.en: Because those 8 control bytes are contiguous, the runtime can inspect all slot states for a group in one tight operation.
sentences.zh: 由于这 8 个控制字节是连续的，因此运行时可以在一次紧密操作中检查一组的所有槽状态。

blocks.html_en: Probe sequence: filter first, compare keys second

sentences.en: Probe sequence: filter first, compare keys second
sentences.zh: 探测顺序：首先过滤，然后比较键

blocks.html_en: Lookup becomes a two-stage loop:

sentences.en: Lookup becomes a two-stage loop:
sentences.zh: 查找变成两阶段循环：

blocks.html_en: • Read the current group's control bytes.

sentences.en: Read the current group's control bytes.
sentences.zh: 读取当前组的控制字节。

blocks.html_en: • Find control-byte positions whose fingerprints match h2.

sentences.en: Find control-byte positions whose fingerprints match h2.
sentences.zh: 查找指纹与 h2 匹配的控制字节位置。

blocks.html_en: • For those positions only, compare real keys.

sentences.en: For those positions only, compare real keys.
sentences.zh: 仅对于这些位置，比较真实的键。

blocks.html_en: • If no match, advance to the next group in the probe sequence.

sentences.en: If no match, advance to the next group in the probe sequence.
sentences.zh: 如果不匹配，则前进到探测序列中的下一组。

blocks.html_en: • Stop when an empty slot proves the key is absent.

sentences.en: Stop when an empty slot proves the key is absent.
sentences.zh: 当空槽证明钥匙不存在时停止。

sentences.en: Simplified pseudocode:
sentences.zh: 简化的伪代码：

blocks.html_en: The hasEmpty(ctrl[g]) check is key. In open addressing, an empty slot means probing can terminate: if the key had ever been inserted along this sequence, the probe would have encountered it before the first truly empty slot.

sentences.en: The hasEmpty(ctrl[g]) check is key.
sentences.zh: hasEmpty(ctrl[g]) 检查是关键。

sentences.en: In open addressing, an empty slot means probing can terminate: if the key had ever been inserted along this sequence, the probe would have encountered it before the first truly empty slot.
sentences.zh: 在开放寻址中，空槽意味着探测可以终止：如果曾经沿着此序列插入密钥，则探测将在第一个真正空槽之前遇到它。

blocks.html_en: Insertion and the role of deleted slots

sentences.en: Insertion and the role of deleted slots
sentences.zh: 插入和删除槽的作用

blocks.html_en: Insert follows the same probe path used by lookup, but it tracks the first reusable position it sees. Reusable can mean either:

sentences.en: Insert follows the same probe path used by lookup, but it tracks the first reusable position it sees.
sentences.zh: 插入遵循查找所使用的相同探测路径，但它跟踪它看到的第一个可重用位置。

sentences.en: Reusable can mean either:
sentences.zh: 可重复使用可能意味着：

blocks.html_en: • an empty slot, or

sentences.en: an empty slot, or
sentences.zh: 一个空槽，或者

blocks.html_en: • a deleted slot (tombstone), depending on policy and probe progress.

sentences.en: a deleted slot (tombstone), depending on policy and probe progress.
sentences.zh: 已删除的槽（逻辑删除），具体取决于策略和探测进度。

blocks.html_en: When lookup fails to find the key, insert writes into the best reusable slot discovered so far. This preserves probe invariants while limiting uncontrolled cluster growth.

sentences.en: When lookup fails to find the key, insert writes into the best reusable slot discovered so far.
sentences.zh: 当查找无法找到密钥时，将写入插入到迄今为止发现的最佳可重用插槽中。

sentences.en: This preserves probe invariants while limiting uncontrolled cluster growth.
sentences.zh: 这保留了探针不变量，同时限制了不受控制的簇增长。

blocks.html_en: Deletion does not usually compact the cluster immediately. Instead, it marks metadata as deleted. Immediate compaction would make single deletes expensive and can break probe continuity guarantees. The trade-off is that too many tombstones can lengthen future probes, so implementations need cleanup behavior during growth or reorganization phases.

sentences.en: Deletion does not usually compact the cluster immediately.
sentences.zh: 删除通常不会立即压缩集群。

sentences.en: Instead, it marks metadata as deleted.
sentences.zh: 相反，它将元数据标记为已删除。

sentences.en: Immediate compaction would make single deletes expensive and can break probe continuity guarantees.
sentences.zh: 立即压缩会使单个删除成本高昂，并且可能破坏探测连续性保证。

sentences.en: The trade-off is that too many tombstones can lengthen future probes, so implementations need cleanup behavior during growth or reorganization phases.
sentences.zh: 代价是太多的墓碑会延长未来的探测时间，因此实现需要在增长或重组阶段进行清理行为。

blocks.html_en: Why this maps well to modern CPUs

sentences.en: Why this maps well to modern CPUs
sentences.zh: 为什么这可以很好地映射到现代 CPU

blocks.html_en: Swiss Tables are often described as "SIMD-friendly," but the broader point is locality plus branch behavior:

sentences.en: Swiss Tables are often described as "SIMD-friendly," but the broader point is locality plus branch behavior:
sentences.zh: 瑞士表通常被描述为“SIMD 友好”，但更广泛的观点是局部性加上分支行为：

blocks.html_en: • Contiguous metadata scan: a group's control bytes are read together, reducing scattered memory touches.

sentences.en: Contiguous metadata scan: a group's control bytes are read together, reducing scattered memory touches.
sentences.zh: 连续元数据扫描：一组控制字节一起读取，减少分散的内存接触。

blocks.html_en: • Fewer full key loads: most slots fail at fingerprint stage, so key comparisons are sparse.

sentences.en: Fewer full key loads: most slots fail at fingerprint stage, so key comparisons are sparse.
sentences.zh: 更少的完整密钥负载：大多数插槽在指纹阶段失败，因此密钥比较稀疏。

blocks.html_en: • Predictable hot loop: probe steps are simple and repetitive, helping branch prediction.

sentences.en: Predictable hot loop: probe steps are simple and repetitive, helping branch prediction.
sentences.zh: 可预测的热循环：探测步骤简单且重复，有助于分支预测。

blocks.html_en: • Better cache residency: metadata and nearby slots are packed to favor cache lines.

sentences.en: Better cache residency: metadata and nearby slots are packed to favor cache lines.
sentences.zh: 更好的缓存驻留：元数据和附近的槽被打包以支持缓存线。

blocks.html_en: Even without architecture-specific vector instructions, this shape tends to perform better than pointer-heavy traversals once maps reach realistic production sizes.

sentences.en: Even without architecture-specific vector instructions, this shape tends to perform better than pointer-heavy traversals once maps reach realistic production sizes.
sentences.zh: 即使没有特定于体系结构的矢量指令，一旦地图达到实际的生产尺寸，这种形状往往比指针密集型遍历表现得更好。

blocks.html_en: Load factor and practical ceiling

sentences.en: Load factor and practical ceiling
sentences.zh: 负载率和实用上限

blocks.html_en: The old bucket-overflow model had to balance overflow growth costs relatively early. Swiss-style open addressing tolerates denser occupancy before performance degrades sharply, because probe work remains mostly linear scans over compact metadata and nearby slots.

sentences.en: The old bucket-overflow model had to balance overflow growth costs relatively early.
sentences.zh: 旧的桶溢出模型必须相对较早地平衡溢出增长成本。

sentences.en: Swiss-style open addressing tolerates denser occupancy before performance degrades sharply, because probe work remains mostly linear scans over compact metadata and nearby slots.
sentences.zh: 瑞士式开放寻址在性能急剧下降之前可以容忍更密集的占用，因为探测工作主要仍然是对紧凑元数据和附近插槽的线性扫描。

blocks.html_en: In practice, this pushes useful load factors upward into the high-80% range (often discussed around 87.5% for 8-slot group designs). The exact threshold is implementation-dependent, but the key result is consistent: denser tables are possible before lookups and inserts become too expensive.

sentences.en: In practice, this pushes useful load factors upward into the high-80% range (often discussed around 87.5% for 8-slot group designs).
sentences.zh: 在实践中，这会将有用的负载系数向上推至 80% 的高范围（对于 8 插槽组设计，通常讨论为 87.5% 左右）。

sentences.en: The exact threshold is implementation-dependent, but the key result is consistent: denser tables are possible before lookups and inserts become too expensive.
sentences.zh: 确切的阈值取决于实现，但关键结果是一致的：在查找和插入变得过于昂贵之前，可以实现更密集的表。

blocks.html_en: Higher usable density means less memory overhead per stored entry and fewer growth events for the same number of elements — both effects that show up directly in heap profiles and allocation rates.

sentences.en: Higher usable density means less memory overhead per stored entry and fewer growth events for the same number of elements — both effects that show up directly in heap profiles and allocation rates.
sentences.zh: 更高的可用密度意味着每个存储条目的内存开销更少，并且相同数量的元素的增长事件更少——这两种影响都直接显示在堆配置文件和分配率中。

blocks.html_en: The trade-offs do not disappear

sentences.en: The trade-offs do not disappear
sentences.zh: 权衡并没有消失

blocks.html_en: Swiss Tables are not universally faster in every corner case. At high tombstone density or under specific delete-heavy patterns, probe lengths can regress until cleanup or growth restores table quality. Extremely adversarial hash distributions still hurt any open-addressing design, even with strong metadata filtering.

sentences.en: Swiss Tables are not universally faster in every corner case.
sentences.zh: Swiss Table 并非在所有极端情况下都普遍更快。

sentences.en: At high tombstone density or under specific delete-heavy patterns, probe lengths can regress until cleanup or growth restores table quality.
sentences.zh: 在高墓碑密度或特定的重删除模式下，探针长度可能会下降，直到清理或增长恢复表质量。

sentences.en: Extremely adversarial hash distributions still hurt any open-addressing design, even with strong metadata filtering.
sentences.zh: 即使有强大的元数据过滤，极端对抗性的哈希分布仍然会损害任何开放寻址设计。

blocks.html_en: The improvement comes from moving the common case onto a much more cache-efficient path, not from eliminating all hard cases.

sentences.en: The improvement comes from moving the common case onto a much more cache-efficient path, not from eliminating all hard cases.
sentences.zh: 改进来自于将常见情况转移到缓存效率更高的路径上，而不是消除所有困难情况。

blocks.html_en: That is why the shift matters so much for Go: maps are used everywhere, and the common case is where most CPU cycles are spent.

sentences.en: That is why the shift matters so much for Go: maps are used everywhere, and the common case is where most CPU cycles are spent.
sentences.zh: 这就是为什么这种转变对于 Go 如此重要：映射无处不在，而且最常见的情况是花费了大部分 CPU 周期。

blocks.html_en: Go-Specific Adaptations

sentences.en: Go-Specific Adaptations
sentences.zh: Go 特定的适应

blocks.html_en: If this were only a straightforward port of Abseil-style Swiss Tables, the runtime work would have been simpler. Go maps, however, have constraints that come from language behavior, GC integration, and long-standing expectations around latency and iteration. The interesting part of Go 1.24 is not just adopting Swiss-style probing, but adapting it so those constraints still hold.

sentences.en: If this were only a straightforward port of Abseil-style Swiss Tables, the runtime work would have been simpler.
sentences.zh: 如果这只是 Abseil 式瑞士表的直接移植，那么运行时工作会更简单。

sentences.en: Go maps, however, have constraints that come from language behavior, GC integration, and long-standing expectations around latency and iteration.
sentences.zh: 然而，Go 映射受到语言行为、GC 集​​成以及对延迟和迭代的长期期望的限制。

sentences.en: The interesting part of Go 1.24 is not just adopting Swiss-style probing, but adapting it so those constraints still hold.
sentences.zh: Go 1.24 的有趣之处不仅在于采用瑞士式探测，还在于对其进行调整，使这些限制仍然存在。

blocks.html_en: Growth without long stop-the-world style spikes

sentences.en: Growth without long stop-the-world style spikes
sentences.zh: 增长不会出现长期停滞式的峰值

blocks.html_en: Classic open-addressing tables are often resized by allocating a larger table and reinserting everything in one large migration step. That is fine in some systems, but Go maps are used on hot request paths where single-operation latency matters. A resize strategy that occasionally performs a full-table rehash can create exactly the kind of long tail the runtime tries to avoid.

sentences.en: Classic open-addressing tables are often resized by allocating a larger table and reinserting everything in one large migration step.
sentences.zh: 经典的开放寻址表通常通过分配一个更大的表并在一个大型迁移步骤中重新插入所有内容来调整大小。

sentences.en: That is fine in some systems, but Go maps are used on hot request paths where single-operation latency matters.
sentences.zh: 这在某些系统中没问题，但 Go 映射用于单操作延迟很重要的热请求路径。

sentences.en: A resize strategy that occasionally performs a full-table rehash can create exactly the kind of long tail the runtime tries to avoid.
sentences.zh: 偶尔执行全表重新哈希的调整大小策略可以准确地创建运行时试图避免的那种长尾。

blocks.html_en: Go's adaptation avoids that monolithic jump by spreading growth across smaller units. Instead of treating the map as one giant table that doubles and fully rehashes at once, the runtime can split work so expansion happens incrementally. Operationally, this keeps mutation costs more stable because a single insert is less likely to inherit the full cost of moving every existing element.

sentences.en: Go's adaptation avoids that monolithic jump by spreading growth across smaller units.
sentences.zh: Go 的适应通过将增长分散到较小的单元来避免整体跳跃。

sentences.en: Instead of treating the map as one giant table that doubles and fully rehashes at once, the runtime can split work so expansion happens incrementally.
sentences.zh: 运行时可以拆分工作，以便增量地进行扩展，而不是将映射视为一个巨大的表，立即加倍并完全重新散列。

sentences.en: Operationally, this keeps mutation costs more stable because a single insert is less likely to inherit the full cost of moving every existing element.
sentences.zh: 从操作上来说，这使突变成本更加稳定，因为单个插入不太可能继承移动每个现有元素的全部成本。

blocks.html_en: The practical effect is similar in spirit to the old map's gradual evacuation model: growth still happens, but migration work is amortized across normal operations rather than concentrated into one expensive event.

sentences.en: The practical effect is similar in spirit to the old map's gradual evacuation model: growth still happens, but migration work is amortized across normal operations rather than concentrated into one expensive event.
sentences.zh: 实际效果在精神上类似于旧地图的逐步疏散模型：增长仍然发生，但迁移工作在正常操作中分摊，而不是集中到一个昂贵的事件中。

blocks.html_en: Multiple independent tables and directory-style routing

sentences.en: Multiple independent tables and directory-style routing
sentences.zh: 多个独立表和目录式路由

blocks.html_en: One of the key Go-specific choices is to organize storage as multiple smaller Swiss-style tables rather than one ever-growing monolith. A higher-level directory (conceptually similar to extendible hashing) routes keys to a specific table segment, and only the segment under pressure needs to split.

sentences.en: One of the key Go-specific choices is to organize storage as multiple smaller Swiss-style tables rather than one ever-growing monolith.
sentences.zh: Go 特定的关键选择之一是将存储组织为多个较小的瑞士式表，而不是一个不断增长的整体。

sentences.en: A higher-level directory (conceptually similar to extendible hashing) routes keys to a specific table segment, and only the segment under pressure needs to split.
sentences.zh: 更高级别的目录（概念上类似于可扩展哈希）将键路由到特定的表段，并且只有处于压力下的段才需要拆分。

blocks.html_en: Keeping growth local means hot key regions can expand without forcing a global rebuild, and bounding memory movement to the splitting segment improves latency predictability under write-heavy bursts.

sentences.en: Keeping growth local means hot key regions can expand without forcing a global rebuild, and bounding memory movement to the splitting segment improves latency predictability under write-heavy bursts.
sentences.zh: 保持本地增长意味着热键区域可以在不强制全局重建的情况下扩展，并且将内存移动限制到分割段可以提高写入大量突发情况下的延迟可预测性。

blocks.html_en: At a conceptual level, insertion looks like this:

sentences.en: At a conceptual level, insertion looks like this:
sentences.zh: 在概念层面上，插入看起来像这样：

blocks.html_en: That directory update is much cheaper than rebuilding every segment, and it composes well with Go's preference for incremental runtime work.

sentences.en: That directory update is much cheaper than rebuilding every segment, and it composes well with Go's preference for incremental runtime work.
sentences.zh: 该目录更新比重建每个段便宜得多，并且它与 Go 对增量运行时工作的偏好很好地结合在一起。

blocks.html_en: Preserving Go's range semantics while tables change

sentences.en: Preserving Go's range semantics while tables change
sentences.zh: 表更改时保留 Go 的范围语义

blocks.html_en: One of the hardest constraints is preserving Go's map iteration behavior while inserts, deletes, and growth are happening.

sentences.en: One of the hardest constraints is preserving Go's map iteration behavior while inserts, deletes, and growth are happening.
sentences.zh: 最难的限制之一是在发生插入、删除和增长时保留 Go 的映射迭代行为。

blocks.html_en: In Go, iterating with range over a map has deliberately loose ordering guarantees, but it still has safety and consistency expectations. The runtime cannot expose torn state, lose reachability to entries that should still be visible under the language rules, or let relocation mechanics violate iterator correctness.

sentences.en: In Go, iterating with range over a map has deliberately loose ordering guarantees, but it still has safety and consistency expectations.
sentences.zh: 在 Go 中，在映射上进行范围迭代故意宽松的排序保证，但它仍然具有安全性和一致性期望。

sentences.en: The runtime cannot expose torn state, lose reachability to entries that should still be visible under the language rules, or let relocation mechanics violate iterator correctness.
sentences.zh: 运行时不能暴露撕裂状态，不能失去对在语言规则下仍然可见的条目的可达性，或者让重定位机制违反迭代器的正确性。

blocks.html_en: With segmented Swiss-style storage, this means iterators must understand that entries may move as segments split or internal probe layouts change. The runtime therefore couples iteration state to map-internal versioning and traversal metadata so the iterator can continue safely even while structure evolves.

sentences.en: With segmented Swiss-style storage, this means iterators must understand that entries may move as segments split or internal probe layouts change.
sentences.zh: 对于分段瑞士式存储，这意味着迭代器必须了解条目可能会随着段的分割或内部探针布局的变化而移动。

sentences.en: The runtime therefore couples iteration state to map-internal versioning and traversal metadata so the iterator can continue safely even while structure evolves.
sentences.zh: 因此，运行时将迭代状态与映射内部版本控制和遍历元数据耦合起来，以便迭代器即使在结构发生变化时也可以安全地继续。

blocks.html_en: The implementation details are complex, but the user-visible result is simple: for k, v := range m keeps working while the runtime earns better cache locality and denser storage under the hood.

sentences.en: The implementation details are complex, but the user-visible result is simple: for k, v := range m keeps working while the runtime earns better cache locality and denser storage under the hood.
sentences.zh: 实现细节很复杂，但用户可见的结果很简单：对于 k, v := range m 继续工作，同时运行时在后台获得更好的缓存局部性和更密集的存储。

blocks.html_en: GC and write-barrier friendliness

sentences.en: GC and write-barrier friendliness
sentences.zh: GC 和写屏障友好性

blocks.html_en: Go cannot treat table entries as purely mechanical bytes. Keys and values may contain pointers, and pointer movement interacts with garbage collection and write barriers. Any redesign of map internals must preserve accurate pointer visibility and barrier behavior during insert, delete, grow, and iterator transitions.

sentences.en: Go cannot treat table entries as purely mechanical bytes.
sentences.zh: Go 不能将表条目视为纯粹的机械字节。

sentences.en: Keys and values may contain pointers, and pointer movement interacts with garbage collection and write barriers.
sentences.zh: 键和值可能包含指针，并且指针移动与垃圾收集和写屏障交互。

sentences.en: Any redesign of map internals must preserve accurate pointer visibility and barrier behavior during insert, delete, grow, and iterator transitions.
sentences.zh: 映射内部的任何重新设计都必须在插入、删除、增长和迭代器转换期间保留准确的指针可见性和屏障行为。

blocks.html_en: Segmented growth helps here too. Smaller relocation steps are easier to integrate with barriered writes and reduce the size of any single pointer-moving operation. This does not remove complexity, but it narrows blast radius and keeps runtime bookkeeping more tractable.

sentences.en: Segmented growth helps here too.
sentences.zh: 分段增长在这里也有帮助。

sentences.en: Smaller relocation steps are easier to integrate with barriered writes and reduce the size of any single pointer-moving operation.
sentences.zh: 较小的重定位步骤更容易与屏障写入集成，并减少任何单个指针移动操作的大小。

sentences.en: This does not remove complexity, but it narrows blast radius and keeps runtime bookkeeping more tractable.
sentences.zh: 这并没有消除复杂性，但它缩小了爆炸半径并使运行时簿记更容易处理。

blocks.html_en: Swiss-style metadata probing delivers the raw algorithmic win, but Go-specific adaptations — segmented growth, iterator-safe migration, and GC-barrier integration — are what make that win usable at scale in a garbage-collected, latency-sensitive runtime. The performance numbers in the next section reflect both layers working together.

sentences.en: Swiss-style metadata probing delivers the raw algorithmic win, but Go-specific adaptations — segmented growth, iterator-safe migration, and GC-barrier integration — are what make that win usable at scale in a garbage-collected, latency-sensitive runtime.
sentences.zh: 瑞士风格的元数据探测带来了原始算法的胜利，但 Go 特定的适应——分段增长、迭代器安全迁移和 GC 屏障集成——使得这一胜利可以在垃圾收集、延迟敏感的运行时中大规模使用。

sentences.en: The performance numbers in the next section reflect both layers working together.
sentences.zh: 下一节中的性能数据反映了两个层的协同工作。

blocks.html_en: Performance & Memory Analysis (Deeper Dive)

sentences.en: Performance & Memory Analysis (Deeper Dive)
sentences.zh: 性能和内存分析（深入探讨）

blocks.html_en: The easiest way to get misled by map benchmarks is to look only at a single synthetic test and assume that number transfers directly to production. For Swiss maps in Go, the public data tells a more nuanced story: the micro-level wins are real and often large, the application-level aggregate win is smaller but still positive, and a few workload shapes do regress enough to deserve attention.

sentences.en: The easiest way to get misled by map benchmarks is to look only at a single synthetic test and assume that number transfers directly to production.
sentences.zh: 被地图基准误导的最简单方法是只查看单个综合测试并假设数字直接转移到生产中。

sentences.en: For Swiss maps in Go, the public data tells a more nuanced story: the micro-level wins are real and often large, the application-level aggregate win is smaller but still positive, and a few workload shapes do regress enough to deserve attention.
sentences.zh: 对于围棋中的瑞士地图，公开数据讲述了一个更微妙的故事：微观层面的胜利是真实的，而且往往很大，应用程序层面的总体胜利较小，但仍然是积极的，一些工作负载形状确实出现了足够的倒退，值得关注。

blocks.html_en: The official release notes for Go 1.24 report that runtime work, including the new Swiss map implementation, lowered CPU overhead by about 2 to 3 percent on average across a representative benchmark suite (Go 1.24 release notes, Runtime section). That is a whole-runtime number, not a map-only number, but it is useful as a reality check because it is measured across mixed workloads.

sentences.en: The official release notes for Go 1.24 report that runtime work, including the new Swiss map implementation, lowered CPU overhead by about 2 to 3 percent on average across a representative benchmark suite (Go 1.24 release notes, Runtime section).
sentences.zh: Go 1.24 的官方发行说明报告称，运行时工作（包括新的瑞士地图实现）在代表性基准测试套件中平均降低了约 2% 到 3% 的 CPU 开销（Go 1.24 发行说明，运行时部分）。

sentences.en: That is a whole-runtime number, not a map-only number, but it is useful as a reality check because it is measured across mixed workloads.
sentences.zh: 这是一个整个运行时的数字，而不是仅映射的数字，但它作为现实检查很有用，因为它是跨混合工作负载进行测量的。

blocks.html_en: For map-focused results, the most concrete summary from the runtime team is in Michael Pratt's closing comment on the Swiss map tracking issue: large-map access and assignment were reported around 30 to 35 percent faster, iteration about 10 percent faster overall and up to about 60 percent faster on low-load large maps, while full-application benchmarks in Sweet showed a geometric-mean speedup around 1.5 percent (golang/go#54766 comment, Sweet benchmark suite).

sentences.en: For map-focused results, the most concrete summary from the runtime team is in Michael Pratt's closing comment on the Swiss map tracking issue: large-map access and assignment were reported around 30 to 35 percent faster, iteration about 10 percent faster overall and up to about 60 percent faster on low-load large maps, while full-application benchmarks in Sweet showed a geometric-mean speedup around 1.5 percent (golang/go#54766 comment, Sweet benchmark suite).
sentences.zh: 对于以地图为中心的结果，运行时团队最具体的总结是 Michael Pratt 对瑞士地图跟踪问题的结束评论：据报告，大地图访问和分配速度提高了约 30% 到 35%，迭代速度总体快了约 10%，在低负载大型地图上速度提高了约 60%，而 Sweet 中的完整应用程序基准测试显示几何平均加速约为 1.5%（golang/go#54766 评论，Sweet 基准测试套件）。

blocks.html_en: That gap between "30 percent here" and "1.5 percent there" is exactly what we should expect. Microbenchmarks isolate map operations, keep code paths hot, and often stress one operation type at a time. Real services spend time in parsing, syscalls, RPC boundaries, scheduling, GC assists, and dozens of non-map code paths, so map wins are diluted unless maps dominate the profile.

sentences.en: That gap between "30 percent here" and "1.5 percent there" is exactly what we should expect.
sentences.zh: “这里 30%”和“那里 1.5%”之间的差距正是我们所期望的。

sentences.en: Microbenchmarks isolate map operations, keep code paths hot, and often stress one operation type at a time.
sentences.zh: 微基准测试隔离映射操作，保持代码路径热度，并且通常一次强调一种操作类型。

sentences.en: Real services spend time in parsing, syscalls, RPC boundaries, scheduling, GC assists, and dozens of non-map code paths, so map wins are diluted unless maps dominate the profile.

blocks.html_en: There is also evidence that benchmark design itself can exaggerate or mask effects. In a follow-up issue about map benchmarking quality, the Go team called out branch-predictor-friendly key patterns, power-of-two map sizes, and benchmark harness overhead as distortions, then showed that changing benchmark structure altered observed deltas substantially (golang/go#70700). One concrete data point from those follow-ups is that a small-map lookup fix for unpredictable keys improved hit latency by roughly 1.7x (about 25ns to about 14ns in the posted numbers), with misses also improving by about 1.3x in the same benchmark set (CL 634396 summary in #70700).

sentences.en: There is also evidence that benchmark design itself can exaggerate or mask effects.
sentences.zh: 还有证据表明基准设计本身可能会夸大或掩盖效果。

blocks.html_en: On memory, two facts are well supported by public sources. First, Swiss-style probing can run at higher practical occupancy than the old overflow-chain design, which tends to reduce per-entry overhead in many cases (Abseil Swiss table design, golang/go#54766). Second, Go's early public Swiss-map benchmark summary reported memory reductions in a broad but workload-dependent range, described there as 0 to 25 percent in most cases, with specific notes about avoiding extra allocations when reusing fixed-size maps (performance summary in #54766).

sentences.en: On memory, two facts are well supported by public sources.
sentences.zh: 据记忆，有两个事实得到了公共资料的充分支持。

sentences.en: First, Swiss-style probing can run at higher practical occupancy than the old overflow-chain design, which tends to reduce per-entry overhead in many cases (Abseil Swiss table design, golang/go#54766).
sentences.zh: 首先，瑞士风格的探测可以比旧的溢出链设计以更高的实际占用率运行，这在许多情况下往往会减少每个条目的开销（Abseil Swiss 表设计，golang/go#54766）。

sentences.en: Second, Go's early public Swiss-map benchmark summary reported memory reductions in a broad but workload-dependent range, described there as 0 to 25 percent in most cases, with specific notes about avoiding extra allocations when reusing fixed-size maps (performance summary in #54766).

blocks.html_en: The cautionary side however, is equally important. The Go team and users tracked several regressions or edge cases after the 1.24 rollout, especially around cold-cache behavior and sparse-large-map patterns. The open cold-cache tracking issue explains why directory indirection and multiple allocations can increase miss costs and discusses layout experiments aimed at that problem (golang/go#70835). A concrete external report in that thread from Prometheus benchmarking showed higher runtime.mapaccess1_fast64 CPU time on Go 1.24.2 versus 1.23 for that workload shape, which is exactly the kind of profile-specific behavior that can hide behind positive geomeans (Prometheus report in #70835).

blocks.html_en: The practical interpretation is straightforward: if your service is lookup- or insert-heavy with medium to large maps, Go 1.24+ likely gives you a free speedup and often better memory efficiency. If your profile is dominated by cold misses, very sparse huge maps, or tight clear/reuse loops, you should measure directly on your workload and watch ongoing runtime work, because those are active optimization areas rather than solved history.

sentences.en: Practical Takeaways for Go Developers
sentences.zh: Go 开发者的实用要点

blocks.html_en: Understanding where the new implementation earns its wins helps you make better profiling decisions, write map-friendly patterns, and calibrate what upgrading to 1.24+ will actually deliver for your specific service.

sentences.en: Understanding where the new implementation earns its wins helps you make better profiling decisions, write map-friendly patterns, and calibrate what upgrading to 1.24+ will actually deliver for your specific service.

blocks.html_en: Where you will see the most impact

sentences.en: Where you will see the most impact
sentences.zh: 您将在哪里看到最大的影响力

blocks.html_en: The gains are largest when maps are the actual bottleneck. Large maps with frequent access are the clearest case: lookup and insert speed up most noticeably once a map has enough entries to expose pointer-chasing and cache-miss costs in the old implementation. A service that maintains large in-memory lookup tables, a cache keyed on structured identifiers, or a concurrent-access pattern over many sharded maps all stand to benefit measurably.

sentences.en: The gains are largest when maps are the actual bottleneck.
sentences.zh: 当地图成为实际瓶颈时，收益最大。

sentences.en: Large maps with frequent access are the clearest case: lookup and insert speed up most noticeably once a map has enough entries to expose pointer-chasing and cache-miss costs in the old implementation.
sentences.zh: 频繁访问的大型映射是最明显的情况：一旦映射有足够的条目来暴露旧实现中的指针追逐和缓存未命中成本，查找和插入速度就会显着提高。

sentences.en: A service that maintains large in-memory lookup tables, a cache keyed on structured identifiers, or a concurrent-access pattern over many sharded maps all stand to benefit measurably.
sentences.zh: 维护大型内存中查找表、基于结构化标识符的缓存或多个分片映射上的并发访问模式的服务都将受益匪浅。

blocks.html_en: Iteration over large but sparsely populated maps also improves significantly. The old design had to walk all buckets regardless of occupancy; Swiss-style control-byte metadata lets the runtime skip empty groups quickly. If your code uses range to scan or drain big maps, that path gets faster.

sentences.en: Iteration over large but sparsely populated maps also improves significantly.
sentences.zh: 对大型但人口稀少的地图的迭代也显着改善。

sentences.en: The old design had to walk all buckets regardless of occupancy; Swiss-style control-byte metadata lets the runtime skip empty groups quickly.
sentences.zh: 旧的设计必须遍历所有的桶，无论占用情况如何；瑞士风格的控制字节元数据让运行时快速跳过空组。

sentences.en: If your code uses range to scan or drain big maps, that path gets faster.
sentences.zh: 如果您的代码使用范围来扫描或耗尽大地图，则该路径会变得更快。

blocks.html_en: Memory-constrained services are another case worth measuring. Higher load factors and the elimination of overflow bucket chains can reduce heap pressure from map storage, which in turn reduces GC frequency and can improve heap efficiency across the board.

sentences.en: Memory-constrained services are another case worth measuring.
sentences.zh: 内存受限服务是另一个值得衡量的案例。

sentences.en: Higher load factors and the elimination of overflow bucket chains can reduce heap pressure from map storage, which in turn reduces GC frequency and can improve heap efficiency across the board.
sentences.zh: 更高的负载因子和消除溢出桶链可以减少映射存储的堆压力，从而降低 GC 频率并全面提​​高堆效率。

blocks.html_en: The gains are smallest for maps that are tiny (a handful of keys), dominated by cold access, or never escape the runtime's fast-path specialization for small integer and string keys. For those maps, the new design may be neutral or show small regressions in some microbenchmarks. In practice, if those maps are not showing up as hotspots in your profiles, the difference is rarely relevant.

sentences.zh: 对于很小（少数键）、以冷访问为主或永远无法逃脱运行时对小整数和字符串键的快速路径专门化的映射来说，收益最小。

sentences.en: For those maps, the new design may be neutral or show small regressions in some microbenchmarks.
sentences.zh: 对于这些地图，新设计可能是中性的，或者在某些微基准测试中显示出小的回归。

sentences.zh: 实际上，如果这些地图没有在您的个人资料中显示为热点，则差异很少相关。

blocks.html_en: Profiling map behavior in your service

sentences.en: Profiling map behavior in your service
sentences.zh: 分析您的服务中的地图行为

blocks.html_en: If maps do appear in CPU profiles, runtime.mapaccess1, runtime.mapassign, runtime.mapiterinit, and related symbols are the functions to watch. A large fraction of CPU time in those symbols combined with a flat or slowly improving heap is a good signal that you are in the "before Swiss tables" performance regime, or that some of the known cold-cache edge cases are affecting you.

sentences.en: If maps do appear in CPU profiles, runtime.mapaccess1, runtime.mapassign, runtime.mapiterinit, and related symbols are the functions to watch.
sentences.zh: 如果映射确实出现在 CPU 配置文件中，则需要观察runtime.mapaccess1、runtime.mapassign、runtime.mapiterinit 和相关符号的函数。

sentences.en: A large fraction of CPU time in those symbols combined with a flat or slowly improving heap is a good signal that you are in the "before Swiss tables" performance regime, or that some of the known cold-cache edge cases are affecting you.
sentences.zh: 这些符号中的大部分 CPU 时间与平坦或缓慢改进的堆相结合是一个很好的信号，表明您处于“瑞士表之前”性能状态，或者某些已知的冷缓存边缘情况正在影响您。

blocks.html_en: For memory, heap profiles can show whether map entries contribute disproportionately to live allocation. Go 1.24+ should help here in many workloads, but if you see large map allocations persisting after keys are deleted, it is worth remembering that Go maps still do not shrink their allocated backing storage after deletions. That has not changed.

sentences.zh: 对于内存，堆配置文件可以显示映射条目是否对实时分配贡献不成比例。

sentences.en: Go 1.24+ should help here in many workloads, but if you see large map allocations persisting after keys are deleted, it is worth remembering that Go maps still do not shrink their allocated backing storage after deletions.
sentences.zh: Go 1.24+ 应该可以在许多工作负载中提供帮助，但是如果您看到删除键后仍然存在大型映射分配，那么值得记住的是，删除后 Go 映射仍然不会缩小其分配的后备存储。

sentences.en: That has not changed.
sentences.zh: 这一点没有改变。

blocks.html_en: A quick way to probe whether maps contribute meaningfully to a benchmark or production workload is to compare go tool pprof profiles between Go 1.23 and 1.24+ builds. The runtime-level speedup is automatic, but quantifying it for your own code tells you whether it is worth emphasizing or ignoring.

sentences.zh: 探究映射是否对基准测试或生产工作负载做出有意义的贡献的一种快速方法是比较 Go 1.23 和 1.24+ 版本之间的 go tool pprof 配置文件。

sentences.en: The runtime-level speedup is automatic, but quantifying it for your own code tells you whether it is worth emphasizing or ignoring.
sentences.zh: 运行时级别的加速是自动的，但是为您自己的代码对其进行量化可以告诉您是否值得强调或忽略它。

blocks.html_en: Delete patterns and the clear idiom

sentences.en: Delete patterns and the clear idiom
sentences.zh: 删除模式和清晰的习语

blocks.html_en: The one code-level pattern worth some thought involves heavy delete usage. If your hot path is a tight loop that repeatedly deletes and reinserts many keys, you are exercising the tombstone path inside each probe group. Swiss-style open addressing handles this correctly, but at high tombstone density probes lengthen until cleanup happens during growth or at table reorganization points. This is the same trade-off that exists in other open-addressing designs, and Go's implementation manages it without application involvement, but it does mean delete-dominated workloads may see less benefit than pure lookup or insert workloads.

sentences.en: The one code-level pattern worth some thought involves heavy delete usage.
sentences.zh: 值得思考的一个代码级模式涉及大量删除的使用。

sentences.en: If your hot path is a tight loop that repeatedly deletes and reinserts many keys, you are exercising the tombstone path inside each probe group.
sentences.zh: 如果您的热路径是一个紧密循环，反复删除并重新插入许多键，则您正在每个探针组内使用逻辑删除路径。

sentences.en: Swiss-style open addressing handles this correctly, but at high tombstone density probes lengthen until cleanup happens during growth or at table reorganization points.
sentences.zh: 瑞士式开放寻址可以正确处理这个问题，但在高逻辑删除密度下，探针会延长，直到在增长期间或表重组点进行清理。

sentences.en: This is the same trade-off that exists in other open-addressing designs, and Go's implementation manages it without application involvement, but it does mean delete-dominated workloads may see less benefit than pure lookup or insert workloads.
sentences.zh: 这与其他开放寻址设计中存在的相同权衡，Go 的实现无需应用程序参与即可管理它，但这确实意味着以删除为主的工作负载可能比纯粹的查找或插入工作负载获得更少的好处。

blocks.html_en: The clear(m) idiom used to wipe and reuse a map is something else to be aware of. Go maps do not shrink their backing storage when cleared, so calling clear on a map that previously grew large does not release that memory. The cost of clear itself is proportional to the number of allocated groups in the current design, which can be expensive for maps that were once large but now hold few entries.

sentences.en: The clear(m) idiom used to wipe and reuse a map is something else to be aware of.
sentences.zh: 用于擦除和重复使用地图的clear(m) 惯用语是另外一个需要注意的事情。

sentences.en: Go maps do not shrink their backing storage when cleared, so calling clear on a map that previously grew large does not release that memory.
sentences.zh: Go 映射在清除时不会收缩其后备存储，因此在之前变大的映射上调用清除不会释放该内存。

sentences.en: The cost of clear itself is proportional to the number of allocated groups in the current design, which can be expensive for maps that were once large but now hold few entries.
sentences.zh: 清除本身的成本与当前设计中分配的组的数量成正比，这对于曾经很大但现在包含很少条目的地图来说可能很昂贵。

blocks.html_en: If you use this pattern with maps that burst to large sizes and then shrink back, consider whether the cleared map's long-term backing size is actually appropriate, or whether creating a fresh map in those cases is preferable.

sentences.en: If you use this pattern with maps that burst to large sizes and then shrink back, consider whether the cleared map's long-term backing size is actually appropriate, or whether creating a fresh map in those cases is preferable.
sentences.zh: 如果您将此模式与突然变大然后缩小的地图一起使用，请考虑已清除的地图的长期支持大小是否实际上合适，或者在这些情况下创建新地图是否更可取。

blocks.html_en: What the runtime might still change

sentences.en: What the runtime might still change
sentences.zh: 运行时可能还会发生什么变化

blocks.html_en: There is ongoing work around map cold-cache behavior. Runtime contributors are actively experimenting with memory layout changes, including separating keys from values within groups (the GOEXPERIMENT=mapsplitgroup experiment tracked in #70835), and the cold-cache issue itself remains open for Go 1.27. These are not user-facing API changes, but they mean the performance profile of maps will continue to evolve.

sentences.en: There is ongoing work around map cold-cache behavior.
sentences.zh: 关于地图冷缓存行为的工作正在进行中。

sentences.en: Runtime contributors are actively experimenting with memory layout changes, including separating keys from values within groups (the GOEXPERIMENT=mapsplitgroup experiment tracked in #70835), and the cold-cache issue itself remains open for Go 1.27.
sentences.zh: 运行时贡献者正在积极尝试内存布局更改，包括将组内的键与值分开（#70835 中跟踪的 GOEXPERIMENT=mapsplitgroup 实验），并且冷缓存问题本身在 Go 1.27 中仍然存在。

sentences.en: These are not user-facing API changes, but they mean the performance profile of maps will continue to evolve.
sentences.zh: 这些不是面向用户的 API 更改，但它们意味着地图的性能概况将继续发展。

blocks.html_en: SIMD-based control-byte scanning, which Abseil's C++ implementation uses on x86, is not currently part of Go's Swiss map path. As noted in the CockroachDB swiss README, implementing the probe loop in pure Go assembly with SIMD has non-trivial overhead from function call boundaries, and the Go team has taken a SWAR (SIMD Within A Register) approach instead. That may change in future versions as Go's assembly model and CPU support evolve.

sentences.en: SIMD-based control-byte scanning, which Abseil's C++ implementation uses on x86, is not currently part of Go's Swiss map path.
